title: A Response Theory Probe for Learned Stochastic AI Simulators, Tested on Lorenz-63

paper.title: A Response Theory Probe for Learned Stochastic AI Simulators, Tested on Lorenz-63
paper.abstract:
Abstract Machine-learning emulators of chaotic and stochastic systems are usually validated on forecast skill and long-run statistics.
Neither certifies that an emulator responds correctly to forcing, the property that projection and attribution studies rely on.
Linear response theory makes this testable: the forced response follows from unperturbed correlations through a generalized fluctuation–dissipation relation, and decomposes over the stochastic Ruelle–Pollicott resonances of the Koopman generator.
Building on the Koopmanism Response framework, we turn this into a calibrated, mode-resolved test for learned surrogates: each surrogate rollout passes or fails each check, and failure rates are compared with those of independent realizations of the true system.
On stochastic Lorenz-63, a three-variable toy model, we evaluate SINDy, an MLP, a reservoir computer, a neural ODE and a neural SDE with learned diffusion, over up to 80 rollouts each. A sparse-regression model with the correct library passes every check at rates consistent with the true system.
Invariant-statistics fidelity and response fidelity dissociate in both directions: a quarter of reservoir-computer rollouts pass every invariant-statistics check and match the static susceptibility χ ⁡ ( 0 ) \chi(0) , yet misrepresent the slow relaxation modes, while the neural ODE and SDE rarely meet the invariant-statistics floor but recover those modes in three quarters of rollouts.
As expected of a time-integrated quantity dominated here by fast relaxation, χ ⁡ ( 0 ) \chi(0) does not separate these cases.
For a fixed network, the training formulation (one-step drift, flow map, or multi-step through the integrator) decides which of these properties it gets right.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction & Motivation
sections.text: Machine learning is now a standard tool for modelling dynamical systems, from sparse regression of governing equations [ 5 ] to reservoir computing [ 22 ] and neural differential equations [ 8 ] . Data-driven weather models such as GraphCast [ 17 ] , FourCastNet [ 23 ] , Pangu-Weather [ 1 ] and Aurora [ 2 ] rival physics-based forecasts at a fraction of the cost. Their validation still rests mainly on forecast skill and long-run statistics, increasingly through benchmarks such as WeatherBench 2 [ 26 ] ; case studies and dynamical tests of their physical behaviour are emerging [ 6 , 12 , 4 ] , but are not yet standard. Both test fidelity to the unperturbed distribution, not how the statistics change under forcing, which is what projection, attribution and the study of tipping points require [ 11 ] : a model can reproduce the invariant measure closely and still misrepresent how it deforms under forcing [ 10 ] . Response theory makes this testable. For a large class of chaotic and stochastic systems, the linear response is a correlation function of the unperturbed dynamics, in the spirit of the generalized fluctuation–dissipation theorem [ 21 , 27 ] , and it decomposes over the stochastic Ruelle–Pollicott (RP) resonances of the Koopman generator and their eigenfunctions [ 7 , 18 ] . The Koopmanism Response framework [ 19 , 30 ] computes these objects from a single unperturbed trajectory with extended dynamic mode decomposition (EDMD), with ResDMD residuals guarding against spurious modes [ 29 , 9 ] , and yields a mode-resolved decomposition of the forced Green’s function [ 20 ] . “Did the model learn the physics?” then becomes a falsifiable question: does a surrogate trained only on unperturbed data carry the correct resonances, eigenfunctions and static susceptibility? Stochastic Lorenz-63 is a three-variable toy model of convection with no spatial structure, and our surrogates are not operational climate emulators: it is a controlled testbed with a known true response, used to map how network design and training formulation shape response fidelity, complementing forced-response studies of neural climate emulators [ 10 ] . We contribute (i) a calibrated evaluation protocol for learned stochastic simulators, in which invariant statistics, the static susceptibility and a mode-resolved eigenfunction test are each applied to every rollout and compared with the false-alarm rate of independent true realizations; (ii) a formulation ladder (one-step drift regression, flow map, multi-step neural ODE, neural SDE with learned diffusion) sharing architecture and data, which isolates the effects of the training target, the multi-step loss and learned noise, complemented by an exploratory causal transformer, the architecture family of current weather emulators; and (iii) evidence that invariant-statistics fidelity and response fidelity dissociate in both directions, which a scalar response summary such as χ ⁡ ( 0 ) \chi(0) cannot detect here but the mode-resolved test does.

sections.heading: Learned surrogates.
sections.text: All models are trained on segments of the same unperturbed master trajectory and rolled out with additive noise (App. C ). (i) SINDy [ 5 , 3 ] with a quadratic library containing the true equations (positive control); (ii) an MLP ( 2 × 64 2\times 64 , tanh) fitted to the drift at Δ ​ t fit = 0.01 \Delta t_{\mathrm{fit}}=0.01{} (MLP-drift) or to the next state (MLP-flow); (iii) a reservoir computer (RC) [ 22 ] fitted as a flow map; (iv) a neural ODE (NODE) [ 8 ] , the same network trained through a differentiable RK4 step on multi-step windows; (v) a neural SDE (NSDE) [ 14 ] , the NODE drift plus a learned diagonal diffusion. All rollouts except the NSDE use the true ς \varsigma , an oracle that favours the surrogates; the NSDE uses no true parameter.

sections.heading: Evaluation protocol.
sections.text: Every surrogate passes through the identical instrument and is compared with a held-out true realization by pass/fail checks in four rungs. (1) Invariant statistics: x x -marginal Wasserstein-1, x x -autocorrelation distance, wing-switch ratio and lobe balance f + f_{+} , each of which must lie within the range (“floor”) reached by 50 independent true realizations. (2) Static susceptibility: χ ⁡ ( 0 ) \chi(0) must lie within the range of 100 true realizations. (3–4) Mode-resolved test, scored separately on the two slow real modes and the four oscillatory ones (Fig. 1 c): for each leading eigenfunction we measure the alignment of the surrogate’s eigenfunction φ ~ \tilde{\varphi} with the reference φ \varphi by the overlap O = | ⟨ φ , φ ~ ⟩ μ 0 | / ( ‖ φ ‖ μ 0 ​ ‖ φ ~ ‖ μ 0 ) ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] O=|\langle\varphi,\tilde{\varphi}\rangle_{\mu_{0}}|/(\|\varphi\|_{\mu_{0}}\|\tilde{\varphi}\|_{\mu_{0}})\in[0,1] , the cosine of the angle between them weighted by the invariant measure ( O = 1 O=1 : same function up to scale). The mode passes if O O exceeds what independent true realizations typically reach, their mean overlap minus three standard deviations (clipped to [ 0.5 , 0.99 ] [0.5,0.99] for the oscillatory modes). A rollout fails a rung if it fails any check in it, and a model’s failure rate on a rung is the fraction of its rollouts that fail. The failure rate of 50 fresh true realizations, scored as a perfect surrogate, is each rung’s false-alarm rate. We call a model’s failure rate consistent with the truth when a Fisher exact test against the true realizations gives p ≥ 0.05 p\geq 0.05{} . sections.heading: 4 Discussion
sections.text: The test is calibrated, not exhaustive: one low-dimensional system, one forcing direction and one observable. Thresholds come from 16 calibration truths; rebuilding the slow-mode thresholds from the 50 fresh truths lowers RC’s slow-mode failure rate from 76% to 55%, and the 0.99 cap decides many oscillatory passes (App. A ). Except for the NSDE, rollouts use the true noise intensity; as a robustness check, SINDy fitted to only 100 time units acquires symmetry-breaking terms (App. C ). Neither invariant statistics nor χ ⁡ ( 0 ) \chi(0) certifies the slow dynamics: a quarter of RC’s rollouts pass both with the wrong slow modes. A one-step drift regressed at a coarse step builds the O ⁡ ( Δ ​ t ) O(\Delta t) secant bias into the model and breaks the attractor. One-step flow maps can match the attractor (RC) yet misplace the slow, weakly damped modes, plausibly because these change little over one step and barely enter a one-step loss. Training on multi-step windows through the integrator (NODE, NSDE) recovers the slow modes in three quarters of rollouts but over-switches; the rollout-fine-tuned transformer shows the same split. Multi-step losses, now common in weather emulators [ 17 , 2 ] , thus appear to carry the slow dynamics, and could be paired with invariant-measure constraints or spectral priors rather than with more flexible architectures. As slow modes govern transitions between the quasi-invariant sets of a metastable system and, for forcings that couple to them, its response, a mode-resolved check, needing one unperturbed trajectory per model, should accompany invariant statistics in validating learned simulators. A natural next step is to test whether these patterns persist in spatially extended systems and for state-of-the-art architectures of current emulators.

sections.heading: Appendix A Operator theory
sections.text: This appendix collects the operator-theoretic objects that the response diagnostic in the main text is built on, following the Koopmanism Response framework [ 30 ] . Standard references for the underlying stochastic-analysis facts are [ 24 ] for the Kolmogorov operator and [ 7 ] for stochastic Ruelle-Pollicott resonances.

sections.heading: A.3 Why the noise: deterministic vs. stochastic spectra
sections.text: The regularization ς > 0 \varsigma>0 in ( 2 ) is operator-theoretic, not cosmetic, and it is what makes the response machinery well posed. The deterministic Lorenz-63 flow carries a singular SRB measure, and its Koopman operator is unitary on L μ 0 2 L^{2}_{\mu_{0}} : the dynamics has already settled onto the attractor, so no decay toward it can be observed and the spectrum sits on the imaginary axis (equivalently, on the unit circle for the time- τ \tau map). Adding non-degenerate noise makes ℒ 0 \mathcal{L}_{0} hypoelliptic, yielding a unique smooth ρ 0 \rho_{0} and a quasi-compact semigroup, so that a discrete set of relaxation modes emerges and the data-driven response reconstruction becomes well posed [ 7 , 30 ] .

sections.heading: A.4 Ruelle-Pollicott resonances and the spectral decomposition
sections.text: Assume 𝐏 \mathbf{P} is quasi-compact, i.e. the eigenvalues of 𝒦 0 \mathcal{K}_{0} with real part above the essential growth bound r ess < 0 r_{\mathrm{ess}}<0 are discrete with finite multiplicity. By the spectral mapping theorem, if λ j \lambda_{j} is an eigenvalue of 𝒦 0 \mathcal{K}_{0} with eigenfunction φ j \varphi_{j} , then e λ j ​ t e^{\lambda_{j}t} is an eigenvalue of P t P_{t} with the same eigenfunction. These discrete eigenvalues { λ j } j ≥ 0 \{\lambda_{j}\}_{j\geq 0} , ordered as λ 0 = 0 > Re ⁡ λ 1 ≥ Re ⁡ λ 2 ≥ ⋯ \lambda_{0}=0>\operatorname{Re}\lambda_{1}\geq\operatorname{Re}\lambda_{2}\geq\cdots , are the (stochastic) Ruelle-Pollicott resonances, and they give a physically meaningful decomposition of the semigroup, e t ​ 𝒦 0 = ∑ j ≥ 0 e λ j ​ t ​ Π j + ℛ ⁡ ( t ) , e^{t\mathcal{K}_{0}}=\sum_{j\geq 0}e^{\lambda_{j}t}\,\Pi_{j}+\mathcal{R}(t), (7) where Π j \Pi_{j} projects onto the eigenspace of λ j \lambda_{j} and ℛ ⁡ ( t ) \mathcal{R}(t) collects the essential-spectrum contribution, whose norm decays and becomes negligible as t → ∞ t\to\infty under quasi-compactness. The resonances are intrinsic relaxation rates: a nonzero imaginary part produces oscillatory correlations, the signature of nonequilibrium dynamics, while the spectral gap γ = − Re ⁡ λ 1 \gamma=-\operatorname{Re}\lambda_{1} controls the slowest decay. An accumulation of resonances toward λ 0 = 0 \lambda_{0}=0 signals diverging sensitivity (critical slowing down). This is the structure a learned surrogate must reproduce, and it is precisely what neither forecast skill nor invariant-measure agreement constrains. sections.heading: Appendix B Response theory
sections.text: We now perturb the stationary dynamics and recall how linear response theory fixes the forced behaviour entirely from unperturbed statistics, through a generalized fluctuation-dissipation relation and the same resonances { λ j } \{\lambda_{j}\} of Appendix A . This is the content that turns “did the surrogate learn the physics?” into a falsifiable spectral question. The formulation follows [ 30 ] .

sections.heading: B.5 Data-driven estimation of Γ \Gamma : Method 3 (integration by parts)
sections.text: The one nontrivial ingredient is the conjugate observable Γ = ℒ p ​ ρ 0 / ρ 0 \Gamma=\mathcal{L}_{p}\rho_{0}/\rho_{0} . [ 30 ] give three routes to G f G_{f} . Methods 1 and 2 build Γ \Gamma by first estimating ρ 0 \rho_{0} (e.g. by binning) and then dividing by it; this is fragile whenever μ 0 \mu_{0} concentrates near a (near-)fractal attractor, exactly the Lorenz-63 situation. Method 3 avoids density estimation altogether. It seeks the μ 0 \mu_{0} -weighted least-squares projection of Γ \Gamma onto the dictionary, 𝐜 = 𝐆 + ​ 𝚫 , Δ i = ⟨ ψ i , Γ ⟩ μ 0 = ∫ ℳ ( 𝐗 ⋅ ∇ ψ i ∗ ) ​ ρ 0 ​ 𝑑 𝐱 ≈ 1 T ​ ∫ 0 T 𝐗 ⁡ ( 𝐱 ⁡ ( t ) ) ⋅ ∇ ψ i ∗ ​ ( 𝐱 ⁡ ( t ) ) ​ 𝑑 t , \mathbf{c}=\mathbf{G}^{+}\boldsymbol{\Delta},\hskip 18.49988pt\Delta_{i}=\langle\psi_{i},\Gamma\rangle_{\mu_{0}}=\int_{\mathcal{M}}\!\big(\mathbf{X}\!\cdot\!\nabla\psi_{i}^{*}\big)\,\rho_{0}\,d\mathbf{x}\;\approx\;\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}\mathbf{X}\big(\mathbf{x}(t)\big)\!\cdot\!\nabla\psi_{i}^{*}\big(\mathbf{x}(t)\big)\,dt, (21) where the middle equality is an integration by parts that moves the derivative off ρ 0 \rho_{0} (boundary terms vanish for the smooth, decaying ρ 0 \rho_{0} ), and the last step replaces the μ 0 \mu_{0} -average by a time average along the same unperturbed trajectory used for EDMD. The coefficients of Γ \Gamma in the eigenfunction basis follow from 𝐜 \mathbf{c} via the left eigenvectors, feeding directly into ( 17 ).

sections.text: We force the x x -equation only, 𝐗 ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) = ( 1 , 0 , 0 ) ⊤ \mathbf{X}(\mathbf{x})=(1,0,0)^{\!\top} , with T ⁡ ( t ) = Θ ⁡ ( t ) T(t)=\Theta(t) , and track f = x f=x . The conjugate observable then simplifies to Γ ( 𝐱 ) = − ∂ x ln ρ 0 ( 𝐱 ) , \Gamma(\mathbf{x})=-\,\partial_{x}\ln\rho_{0}(\mathbf{x}), (22) and the Method 3 moments ( 21 ) reduce to Δ i ≈ 1 T ​ ∫ 0 T ∂ x ψ i ∗ ​ ( 𝐱 ⁡ ( t ) ) ​ 𝑑 t \Delta_{i}\approx\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}\partial_{x}\psi_{i}^{*}(\mathbf{x}(t))\,dt . We force x x because it is the most strongly coupled variable, driving both y y and z z through the nonlinear terms, so a single-component forcing maximally probes the cross-variable response and is the cleanest first stress test of the framework. The reference response is the instrument reconstruction on the held-out true realization (seed 101).

sections.heading: B.7 Why the response is a stringent diagnostic
sections.text: Equations ( 16 )-( 17 ) show that the entire forced response is determined by unperturbed objects: the resonances { λ j } \{\lambda_{j}\} , their eigenfunctions φ j \varphi_{j} , and the projection of the intrinsic conjugate observable Γ \Gamma . None of these is constrained by a short-horizon forecast loss or by agreement of the invariant measure. A surrogate trained only on unperturbed data can therefore match the attractor, the wing-switching statistics, and even the scalar χ ⁡ ( 0 ) \chi(0) , while still carrying the wrong eigenfunction structure, a discrepancy that only the mode-resolved test of Appendix A.6 , applied through this response machinery, resolves. Response theory thus supplies a rigorous, physically grounded criterion for whether a learned simulator respects dynamical structure rather than merely fitting the attractor.

sections.heading: C.1 SINDy
sections.text: We fit the drift by sequentially thresholded least squares (STLSQ) on a polynomial library of degree 2, with threshold 0.1 on standardized columns. Under Euler-Maruyama the one-step increment of ( 2 ) at the raw step satisfies 𝔼 ⁡ [ Δ ​ x / Δ ​ t ∣ x ] = F ⁡ ( x ) \mathbb{E}[\Delta x/\Delta t\mid x]=F(x) , so regressing increments on state recovers the drift with the noise averaged out [ 3 ] ; at a coarser step its conditional mean is the secant drift (App. C.2 ). The library contains the true Lorenz-63 equations, so SINDy is a positive control on the whole pipeline rather than a competitive baseline: if the instrument cannot certify a model whose functional form is exactly right, nothing else it reports is trustworthy. The positive control is SINDy trained on the same 10000 time units of the master as the neural models, at the raw step. As a robustness check on record length we also report a fit on 100 time units (SINDy-100); for transparency, this shorter fit was the control before the master trajectory was refitted, and the full-record fit replaced it after the results were seen. Trained on 100 time units instead, SINDy acquires symmetry-breaking constant terms that skew the lobes ( f + = 0.416 f_{+}=0.416 ); it fails invariant statistics in every rollout yet passes both slow modes in every rollout, the converse of the dissociation in Sec. 3 . sections.heading: C.2 MLP
sections.text: The MLP is a map ℝ 3 → ℝ 3 \mathbb{R}^{3}\to\mathbb{R}^{3} with 2 hidden tanh layers of width 64 and standardized inputs and outputs, trained with Adam (learning rate 10 − 3 10^{-3}{} , batch 2048) [ 15 ] on the mean-squared error, with early stopping on a random 10% validation split (patience 5, at most 25 epochs). It is trained on 10000 time units of the master at Δ ​ t fit = 0.01 \Delta t_{\mathrm{fit}}=0.01{} , either on the increment Δ ​ x / Δ ​ t \Delta x/\Delta t (MLP-drift) or on the next state (MLP-flow); the two share data, architecture and seed, so the target is the only difference. A pre-refit sweep over width and depth did not reduce the drift error. At Δ ​ t fit \Delta t_{\mathrm{fit}} the conditional mean of Δ ​ x / Δ ​ t \Delta x/\Delta t is not F F but the secant drift F + ( Δ ​ t / 2 ) ​ J F ​ F + O ⁡ ( Δ ​ t 2 ) F+(\Delta t/2)\,J_{F}F+O(\Delta t^{2}) (the Itô term ς 2 2 ​ ∇ 2 ​ F \tfrac{\varsigma^{2}}{2}\nabla^{2}F vanishes because each component of the Lorenz-63 drift is at most bilinear), and the drift MLP learns it: its error against F F matches the secant bias of its target to within 7.21% per component (Table 11 ). sections.heading: C.3 Reservoir Computing
sections.text: The reservoir is a leaky echo-state network [ 13 ] with N = 1000 N=1000{} units, spectral radius 1, leak rate 0.3, input scaling 0.5, washout 1000 steps and ridge readout regularization 10 − 4 10^{-4}{} , trained on 2000 time units of the master at Δ ​ t fit = 0.02 \Delta t_{\mathrm{fit}}=0.02{} and advanced as a native flow map with injected noise. Like every other surrogate, it is trained on the Euler–Maruyama master, i.e. on noisy data from the stochastic system; its hyperparameters were not retuned for it. The configuration was selected on valid-prediction horizon against a reference trajectory of the deterministic Lorenz-63 system, subject to an attractor gate (bounded, bimodal, plausible wing-switch ratio); response metrics were never used for selection. Two implementation faults had to be fixed first, both of which silently degrade the attractor rather than failing loudly: an off-by-one in the closed-loop rollout seed, and a washout discontinuity in which warm-up ended at the last training state while the rollout restarted from the first. Current RC results are in Tables 1 , 8 and 2 .

sections.heading: C.5 Exploratory: a causal transformer flow map
sections.text: Transformer weather emulators such as Pangu-Weather [ 1 ] , FourCastNet [ 23 ] and Aurora [ 2 ] are, in the taxonomy of Sec. 2 , learned one-step flow maps rolled out autoregressively, with attention mixing spatial tokens. A three-variable system has no spatial tokens, so the analogue we can test here is attention over time. As an exploratory model, with a configuration fixed before the run and no tuning, we add a decoder-only causal transformer [ 28 , 25 , 31 ] that maps the last 16 states to the next-state increment (embedding dimension 64, 2 layers, 4 heads, 68,547 parameters). It is trained on the MLP-flow data with a teacher-forced one-step loss, then fine-tuned on 8-step autoregressive rollouts, as recent emulators are [ 17 , 2 ] , and rolled out with the same oracle noise as MLP-flow. Because the true state is fully observed and Markov, the context cannot improve the one-step prediction: the model is a sequence model with memory, like RC, not a stand-in for spatial-attention emulators. It passed the smoke-test gate fixed in advance, and all 80 rollouts over 8 training × \times 10 rollout seeds were scored, none diverging. Its pattern matches NODE and NSDE (Table 8 ). It fails invariant statistics in 79% of rollouts but the slow modes in only 19%, and the oscillatory modes in 73%, mostly through the individual near-degenerate eigenvectors, while recovering their joint subspace (merged-subspace failure rate 15%; Table 2 ). Of its rollouts, 17 lie inside all four invariant-statistics floors and the χ ⁡ ( 0 ) \chi(0) band, and 2 of these fail the slow-mode test. It differs from MLP-flow in both architecture and the rollout fine-tuning, so its improvement over MLP-flow cannot be attributed to either alone. That it, like the NODE, was trained on multi-step rollouts is consistent with the training formulation, rather than the architecture, setting which properties a model gets right.

China Email: v.lucarini@leicester.ac.uk Francisco Camara Pereira Affiliation: Department of Technology, Affiliation: Management and Economics Affiliation: Technical University of Denmark Affiliation: Kongens Lyngby, 2800, DK Email: camara@dtu.dk Abstract Machine-learning emulators of chaotic and stochastic systems are usually validated on forecast skill and long-run statistics. Neither certifies that an emulator responds correctly to forcing, the property that projection and attribution studies rely on. Linear response theory makes this testable: the forced response follows from unperturbed correlations through a generalized fluctuation–dissipation relation, and decomposes over the stochastic Ruelle–Pollicott resonances of the Koopman generator. Building on the Koopmanism Response framework, we turn this into a calibrated, mode-resolved test for learned surrogates: each surrogate rollout passes or fails each check, and failure rates are compared with those of independent realizations of the true system. On stochastic Lorenz-63, a three-variable toy model, we evaluate SINDy, an MLP, a reservoir computer, a neural ODE and a neural SDE with learned diffusion, over up to 80 rollouts each. A sparse-regression model with the correct library passes every check at rates consistent with the true system. Invariant-statistics fidelity and response fidelity dissociate in both directions: a quarter of reservoir-computer rollouts pass every invariant-statistics check and match the static susceptibility χ ⁡ ( 0 ) \chi(0) , yet misrepresent the slow relaxation modes, while the neural ODE and SDE rarely meet the invariant-statistics floor but recover those modes in three quarters of rollouts. As expected of a time-integrated quantity dominated here by fast relaxation, χ ⁡ ( 0 ) \chi(0) does not separate these cases. For a fixed network, the training formulation (one-step drift, flow map, or multi-step through the integrator) decides which of these properties it gets right. 1 Introduction & Motivation Machine learning is now a standard tool for modelling dynamical systems, from sparse regression of governing equations [ 5 ] to reservoir computing [ 22 ] and neural differential equations [ 8 ] . Data-driven weather models such as GraphCast [ 17 ] , FourCastNet [ 23 ] , Pangu-Weather [ 1 ] and Aurora [ 2 ] rival physics-based forecasts at a fraction of the cost. Their validation still rests mainly on forecast skill and long-run statistics, increasingly through benchmarks such as WeatherBench 2 [ 26 ] ; case studies and dynamical tests of their physical behaviour are emerging [ 6 , 12 , 4 ] , but are not yet standard. Both test fidelity to the unperturbed distribution, not how the statistics change under forcing, which is what projection, attribution and the study of tipping points require [ 11 ] : a model can reproduce the invariant measure closely and still misrepresent how it deforms under forcing [ 10 ] . Response theory makes this testable. For a large class of chaotic and stochastic systems, the linear response is a correlation function of the unperturbed dynamics, in the spirit of the generalized fluctuation–dissipation theorem [ 21 , 27 ] , and it decomposes over the stochastic Ruelle–Pollicott (RP) resonances of the Koopman generator and their eigenfunctions [ 7 , 18 ] . The Koopmanism Response framework [ 19 , 30 ] computes these objects from a single unperturbed trajectory with extended dynamic mode decomposition (EDMD), with ResDMD residuals guarding against spurious modes [ 29 , 9 ] , and yields a mode-resolved decomposition of the forced Green’s function [ 20 ] . “Did the model learn the physics?” then becomes a falsifiable question: does a surrogate trained only on unperturbed data carry the correct resonances, eigenfunctions and static susceptibility? Stochastic Lorenz-63 is a three-variable toy model of convection with no spatial structure, and our surrogates are not operational climate emulators: it is a controlled testbed with a known true response, used to map how network design and training formulation shape response fidelity, complementing forced-response studies of neural climate emulators [ 10 ] . We contribute (i) a calibrated evaluation protocol for learned stochastic simulators, in which invariant statistics, the static susceptibility and a mode-resolved eigenfunction test are each applied to every rollout and compared with the false-alarm rate of independent true realizations; (ii) a formulation ladder (one-step drift regression, flow map, multi-step neural ODE, neural SDE with learned diffusion) sharing architecture and data, which isolates the effects of the training target, the multi-step loss and learned noise, complemented by an exploratory causal transformer, the architecture family of current weather emulators; and (iii) evidence that invariant-statistics fidelity and response fidelity dissociate in both directions, which a scalar response summary such as χ ⁡ ( 0 ) \chi(0) cannot detect here but the mode-resolved test does. 2 Method System and response instrument. Forcings or observables coupled to lobe occupation may load on exactly these modes; the resonances and eigenfunctions, unlike χ ⁡ ( 0 ) \chi(0) , do not depend on that choice. 4 Discussion The test is calibrated, not exhaustive: one low-dimensional system, one forcing direction and one observable. Thresholds come from 16 calibration truths; rebuilding the slow-mode thresholds from the 50 fresh truths lowers RC’s slow-mode failure rate from 76% to 55%, and the 0.99 cap decides many oscillatory passes (App. A ). Except for the NSDE, rollouts use the true noise intensity; as a robustness check, SINDy fitted to only 100 time units acquires symmetry-breaking terms (App. C ). Neither invariant statistics nor χ ⁡ ( 0 ) \chi(0) certifies the slow dynamics: a quarter of RC’s rollouts pass both with the wrong slow modes. A one-step drift regressed at a coarse step builds the O ⁡ ( Δ ​ t ) O(\Delta t) secant bias into the model and breaks the attractor. One-step flow maps can match the attractor (RC) yet misplace the slow, weakly damped modes, plausibly because these change little over one step and barely enter a one-step loss. Training on multi-step windows through the integrator (NODE, NSDE) recovers the slow modes in three quarters of rollouts but over-switches; the rollout-fine-tuned transformer shows the same split. Multi-step losses, now common in weather emulators [ 17 , 2 ] , thus appear to carry the slow dynamics, and could be paired with invariant-measure constraints or spectral priors rather than with more flexible architectures. As slow modes govern transitions between the quasi-invariant sets of a metastable system and, for forcings that couple to them, its response, a mode-resolved check, needing one unperturbed trajectory per model, should accompany invariant statistics in validating learned simulators. A natural next step is to test whether these patterns persist in spatially extended systems and for state-of-the-art architectures of current emulators. References [1] K. Bi, L. Xie, H. Zhang, X. A.3 Why the noise: deterministic vs. stochastic spectra The regularization ς > 0 \varsigma>0 in ( 2 ) is operator-theoretic, not cosmetic, and it is what makes the response machinery well posed. The deterministic Lorenz-63 flow carries a singular SRB measure, and its Koopman operator is unitary on L μ 0 2 L^{2}_{\mu_{0}} : the dynamics has already settled onto the attractor, so no decay toward it can be observed and the spectrum sits on the imaginary axis (equivalently, on the unit circle for the time- τ \tau map).
